67:
In the study "Applying the E-learning Framework: Evaluating an E-learning Course toward the Improvement of Quality of ODeL Programs," Myra D. Oruga and Jelaine R. Bagos examine the complexities of evaluating Open and Distance E-learning (ODeL) environments. The researchers applied the "Evaluation Dimension" of Khan’s Eight-Dimensional E-Learning Framework to assess the course IH 213 (Health Promotion for Equity and Sustainable Development) at the University of the Philippines Open University. The study aimed to evaluate the course's relevance to learners, reflective thinking, interactivity, tutor support, peer support, and the interpretation of messages.

Using a survey research design, data were collected from thirty-three international health learners via an online questionnaire. The findings revealed that the e-learning course was perceived as highly effective in most dimensions. Students reported that the content was relevant to professional practice and that they engaged in critical thinking. Furthermore, tutor support, peer support, and the clarity of messages were rated highly.

However, interactivity was identified as a relative weakness, as students reported only "sometimes" asking classmates to explain ideas or responding to their ideas. This suggests that active interaction between learners is lower than other metrics. The authors conclude that while the course is effective in most areas, interactivity requires improvement. They recommend implementing graded discussion forums, incentives for participation, or activities like debates to enhance the quality of the ODeL program.
